title: The SR Latch: Two Gates Remembering a Bit
excerpt: Two cross-coupled gates are the smallest circuit that can store a single bit,  and the first place you'll meet a genuinely forbidden input.

body.text: The SR Latch: Two Gates Remembering a Bit

content.text: The SR latch is the simplest circuit that can genuinely store a bit, and it needs exactly two gates. Take two NOR gates. Wire the first gate's output into the second gate's input, and the second gate's output back into the first gate's input. That's the whole circuit,  no other components, just two gates pointing at each other in a loop, which is exactly the feedback idea from the last tutorial made concrete.

The two remaining free inputs, one on each gate, are called S (set) and R (reset), and the two gate outputs are called Q and Q̄ ("Q-bar"),  Q̄ is meant to always sit at the opposite value from Q. Whatever Q currently holds
the stored bit. There's no separate memory cell tucked away somewhere; the bit is nothing more than whichever value the loop has settled into.
This version is NOR-based and active-high, meaning a HIGH on an input is what triggers it, which makes the four cases easy to state plainly:
• S = 1, R = 0: Q is forced to 1 ("set").
• S = 0, R = 1: Q is forced to 0 ("reset").
• S = 0, R = 0: Q keeps whatever it was already holding. This is the memory,  neither input is asking for anything, so the loop just maintains its last decision forever.

• S = 1, R = 1: forbidden. Both gates are simultaneously being told to force their output the same way, Q and Q̄ stop being opposites, and the moment you drop back to S = 0, R = 0, which value it settles into depends on which gate happened to react a hair faster, not on anything you control.

Below is the actual circuit,  two real NOR gates, wired exactly the way it was just described, not a stand-in. Click S or R to toggle them and watch the wires themselves light up as the signal propagates through the loop. It's running the same gate-evaluation functions (evaluateNor and friends) that the real Nandscape simulator runs, so what you see here is exactly what the engine would do too. Use "Zoom in" if you want a bigger view of the wiring.

S = 1, R = 1 isn't a case the designer of an SR latch chooses to leave unhandled,  it's structurally impossible to handle. Both NOR gates are wired to actively drive their outputs low, which directly contradicts the whole premise that Q and Q̄ are supposed to disagree. There's no clever gate arrangement that fixes this while keeping two independent set/reset inputs; the fix, as it turns out, is to stop giving the user two independent inputs at all. That's exactly what the next tutorial does.

This exact idea,  two cross-coupled gates holding a bit through feedback,  is the seed every other storage element in this section grows out of. The version you just played with uses NOR gates and active-high inputs because that's the clearest one to reason about first. A second, equally common flavor swaps in NAND gates and flips the inputs to active-low (pulse S
to set, pulse R low to reset, hold both high to remember),  and you'll find that exact variant, built from nothing but real NAND gates, in the sandbox's default circuits and in the puzzle below.

An SR latch asks the person driving it to keep two separate inputs mutually exclusive by hand, forever, or risk the forbidden state. The gated D latch removes that burden entirely by giving you exactly one data input, so there's no combination of inputs left to forbid.
